newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Parliament, politics to influence Ukraine hryvnia.
newsitem.headline: Parliament, politics to influence Ukraine hryvnia.

text.p: Ukraine's hryvnia currency, which has eased back after a steep climb, is likely to hold steady for now but its future course will depend on parliament's approval of new tax laws, analysts said on Friday.

One economist said markets would wait to see if Ukraine adopted new legislation to underpin the 1997 budget, crucial for International Monetary Fund approval of a $2.5 to $3 billion, three-year loan, before deciding whether to move the hryvnia.
"Mid-March is the key date for the programme of reforms," said the economist, who asked not be named.
"If there is clear adoption, the EFF will be signed," he said, referring to an IMF extended fund facility. "If they postpone adoption, the hryvnia could go down."
The hryvnia slipped to 1.8365 to the dollar on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange on Friday from 1.8360 on Thursday and 1.7650 last Friday.
The currency was introduced at 1.76 to the dollar in September 1996 and reached a record low of 1.8938 last month.

The economist said this week's sackings of three ministers, including those holding the finance and economy portfolios, had contributed to the drop in the currency, which started this week at 1.791. New ministers have since been appointed.
"I don't see volatility in the economy causing this. The market is reacting to a lot of change, to political instability" he said.
But Ukrainian dealers said the hryvnia's recent ups and downs made it impossible to predict which way it would go next, especially since high demand on the exchange failed to push it up on Friday.
Serhiy Ponomarenko of Pravexbank said speculative capital was pushing up volumes on the exchange and much money was going into Treasury bills -- which yield up to 38 percent.
"When the hryvnia was going up in value, it was evident that it was because of money being put into T-bills. But now the market is at a crossroads," he said.

Analysts said they suspected that the Ukrainian central bank was intervening to influence the foreign exchange market and one suggested that Ukraine would attempt to fix the hryvnia within a trading band of 1.80 to 1.90 to the dollar.
"No one wants to have it too high because then it hurts exports. No central bank would say it is intervening but it's no secret they're looking for currency stability," said a Western diplomat.
Several former Soviet republics have pegged their currrencies against the dollar, the mark or against a basket of currencies in an effort to control inflation.
The Russian central bank holds the rouble within a gently sloping corridor against the dollar.
The diplomat said the new ministerial appointments might contribute to the hryvnia's stability in the longer term.

"It could, because the new ministers are more credible. A couple of them are real reformers. So it's not just (Deputy Prime Minister of Economy Viktor) Pynzenyk," he said, referring to the minister in charge of reforms.
